### Target 5: Monte Carlo simulation

The paper represents "the mean results of each experiment as a 25-dimensional vector (five
emotions × five sliders), where each dimension has a range from 0.0 to 2.0". It then samples "the
space uniformly at random, generating one-million pairs", and compares the US–Kreung distance with
the distribution of distances between the random pairs. Here the mean vectors come from the
discrete data with music and movement pooled (**D8**), and the null distribution is continuous
uniform (**D9**) with a fixed seed (**D10**).

```{r}
#| label: analysis-montecarlo
# 25-d mean vectors (5 emotions x 5 sliders) of the discrete data, music and movement pooled
mean_vecs <- s2 |>
  group_by(population, emotion) |>
  summarise(across(all_of(sliders), mean), .groups = "drop")
v_us     <- mean_vecs |> filter(population == "us")     |> select(all_of(sliders)) |> as.matrix()
v_kreung <- mean_vecs |> filter(population == "kreung") |> select(all_of(sliders)) |> as.matrix()
d_obs <- sqrt(sum((v_us - v_kreung)^2))
d_obs

# Null: distances between pairs of 25-d vectors drawn uniformly from [0, width]^25.
# Summing squared differences one dimension at a time keeps memory small.
sim_distances <- function(n_pairs, width) {
  d2 <- numeric(n_pairs)
  for (j in 1:25) d2 <- d2 + (runif(n_pairs, 0, width) - runif(n_pairs, 0, width))^2
  sqrt(d2)
}
set.seed(20130102)
null_02 <- sim_distances(1e6, width = 2)  # the range the paper states (0.0 to 2.0)
null_04 <- 2 * null_02                    # a [0, 4] draw is exactly 2 x a [0, 2] draw

mc_tab <- tibble(
  version  = c("Paper", "Stated range, 0 to 2", "Doubled: 0 to 4 (every distance × 2)"),
  observed = c(4.24, d_obs, 2 * d_obs),
  null_mean = c(8.11, mean(null_02), mean(null_04)),
  null_sd  = c(0.97, sd(null_02), sd(null_04)),
  z        = c(3.98, (mean(null_02) - d_obs) / sd(null_02), (mean(null_04) - 2 * d_obs) / sd(null_04)),
  pairs_at_least_as_close = c("fewer than 30", sum(null_02 <= d_obs), sum(null_04 <= 2 * d_obs)))
mc_tab |> kable(digits = 2, caption = "Monte Carlo: paper vs. reproduced (1,000,000 random pairs)")

# The count of close pairs is random: repeat with 20 more seeds
set.seed(1)
close_counts <- replicate(20, sum(sim_distances(1e6, width = 2) <= d_obs))
summary(close_counts)

# Alternative null (D9): discrete uniform on {0, 1, 2}
set.seed(2)
null_disc <- sqrt(rowSums((matrix(sample(0:2, 25 * 1e5, TRUE), ncol = 25) -
                           matrix(sample(0:2, 25 * 1e5, TRUE), ncol = 25))^2))
c(mean = mean(null_disc), sd = sd(null_disc))

ggplot(tibble(distance = null_04), aes(distance)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.1, fill = "grey70", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 2 * d_obs, linewidth = 1) +
  annotate("text", x = 2 * d_obs, y = Inf, label = sprintf("%.2f", 2 * d_obs), vjust = 1.5, hjust = -0.1) +
  labs(title = "Null distribution on the doubled (0–4) scale, as in the paper's Fig. 4",
       x = "Distance", y = "Frequency") +
  theme_minimal()
```

The standardized result reproduces: on the stated 0–2 scale the observed distance is
`r sprintf("%.2f", d_obs)` against a null of mean `r sprintf("%.2f", mean(null_02))` and SD
`r sprintf("%.2f", sd(null_02))`, so *z* = `r sprintf("%.2f", (mean(null_02) - d_obs) / sd(null_02))`.
Only `r sum(null_02 <= d_obs)` of the 1,000,000 pairs were as close; across 20 more seeds the count
ranged from `r min(close_counts)` to `r max(close_counts)` (mean `r sprintf("%.1f", mean(close_counts))`),
which is in line with "fewer than 30". The raw distances do not match the paper: all three
(observed, null mean, null SD) are exactly half the paper's values. The paper's numbers are what you
get when every dimension spans 0–4, or equivalently when every distance is doubled (**D9**). The
paper's Fig. 4 axis (4 to 12) is on that doubled scale as well. Once doubled, the observed distance
is `r sprintf("%.2f", 2 * d_obs)` against the reported 4.24, a difference of 0.01 that I could not
remove with any variant I tried (rounded means, Table S1 Kreung means, unweighted modality means).

### Target 6: distance to United States prototypes

The paper derived US prototypes by "selecting the median value for each slider for each emotion
(for music and movement combined) from the United States results and mapping those values to the
closest Kreung setting" (**D11**). It then "measured the similarity of each of the Kreung
datapoints to the corresponding United States prototype by calculating the Euclidean distance". I
read that as follows: for each Kreung emotion, average each response's distance to each prototype,
and call the emotion matched if its own prototype has the smallest average (**D12**).

```{r}
#| label: analysis-prototypes
# US prototypes: median of the continuous US data per emotion x slider (music + movement),
# snapped to the nearest Kreung setting in Table S4 (0 = low, 1 = medium, 2 = high)
us_medians <- s1 |> group_by(emotion) |> summarise(across(all_of(sliders), median))
prototypes <- us_medians |>
  mutate(across(all_of(sliders), \(x) nearest_level(x, s4_levels[[cur_column()]])))
us_medians |> kable(caption = "US medians (continuous units)")
prototypes |> kable(caption = "US prototypes (0 = low, 1 = medium, 2 = high)")
# Paper: sad median rate = 46 BPM; sad prototype = low rate, low jitter, medium consonance,
# low step size, high (downward) direction
stopifnot(us_medians$bpm[us_medians$emotion == "sad"] == 46,
          all(prototypes[prototypes$emotion == "sad", sliders] == c(0, 0, 1, 0, 2)),
          !anyNA(prototypes))

proto_mat <- prototypes |> select(all_of(sliders)) |> as.matrix()
rownames(proto_mat) <- prototypes$emotion
# Euclidean distance from each row of X (5 slider values) to each of the 5 prototypes
dist_to_protos <- function(X) t(apply(X, 1, function(v) sqrt(colSums((t(proto_mat) - v)^2))))

kreung  <- filter(s2, population == "kreung")
subsets <- list(combined = c("music", "motion"), music = "music", movement = "motion")

# method "mean_of_distances": average over responses of response-to-prototype distance (D12)
# method "distance_of_mean":  distance from the Kreung mean vector to each prototype (alternative)
proto_results <- function(method) {
  imap_dfr(subsets, function(mods, subset_name) {
    map_dfr(emotions, function(e) {
      X <- kreung |> filter(modality %in% mods, emotion == e) |> select(all_of(sliders)) |> as.matrix()
      d <- if (method == "mean_of_distances") colMeans(dist_to_protos(X))
           else dist_to_protos(matrix(colMeans(X), nrow = 1))[1, ]
      names(d) <- rownames(proto_mat)
      ord <- sort(d)
      tibble(subset = subset_name, kreung_emotion = e, closest = names(ord)[1], second = names(ord)[2],
             dist_own = d[[e]], dist_nearest_other = min(d[names(d) != e]))
    })
  }) |> mutate(matched = closest == kreung_emotion, margin = dist_nearest_other - dist_own)
}
proto_counts <- function(res) {
  res |>
    mutate(subset = factor(subset, levels = names(subsets))) |>
    group_by(subset) |>
    summarise(n_matched = sum(matched),
              matched = paste(kreung_emotion[matched], collapse = ", "),
              not_matched = paste(kreung_emotion[!matched], collapse = ", "))
}

proto_main <- proto_results("mean_of_distances")
proto_main |> kable(digits = 3, caption = "Mean distance from Kreung responses to US prototypes (D12)")
proto_main_counts <- proto_counts(proto_main)
proto_main_counts |>
  mutate(paper = c("4 of 5 (all but angry)", "3 of 5 (happy, sad, scared)", "4 of 5 (all but angry)")) |>
  kable(caption = "Kreung emotions closest to the matching US prototype: reproduced vs. paper")

# Alternative (D12): distance from the Kreung mean vector
proto_alt <- proto_results("distance_of_mean")
proto_alt_counts <- proto_counts(proto_alt)
proto_alt_counts |> kable(caption = "Alternative: distance from the Kreung mean vector")
```

```{r}
#| label: prototype-details
#| include: false
pm <- function(sub, emo, col) filter(proto_main, subset == sub, kreung_emotion == emo)[[col]]
```

All three target counts reproduce under D12. On combined data, every emotion except angry is closest
to its own US prototype. Movement alone gives the same result. On music alone, happy, sad and
scared match. The failures also follow the paper. Kreung angry music is closest to the US
`r pm("music", "angry", "closest")` prototype, and angry movement is closest to
`r pm("movement", "angry", "closest")`. Kreung peaceful music is closest to the US
`r pm("music", "peaceful", "closest")` prototype. One detail differs. The paper says peaceful music
was "second closest to the United States 'peaceful' prototype", but here the second closest is
`r pm("music", "peaceful", "second")`.

The counts are fragile. Combined peaceful beats its nearest rival by only
`r sprintf("%.3f", pm("combined", "peaceful", "margin"))`, and movement scared by only
`r sprintf("%.3f", pm("movement", "scared", "margin"))`. That fragility shows in the alternative
reading: with the distance from the Kreung mean vector to each prototype, combined drops to
`r proto_alt_counts$n_matched[1]` of 5 and movement to `r proto_alt_counts$n_matched[3]` of 5,
because peaceful no longer matches in either. Music stays at `r proto_alt_counts$n_matched[2]` of 5.

### Analysis decisions {#analysis-decisions}

The paper and SI leave the following choices open. For each one: what I chose, why, and what
happens under a reasonable alternative.

```{r}
#| label: sensitivity
# --- Targets 1-3 under alternative choices (D1, D3, D4)
us_drop <- us_long |> filter(!str_detect(pid, "^MoMR")) |> droplevels()           # D1: drop both MoMR blocks
us_avg  <- s1 |>                                                                   # D1: MoMR as one person (average)
  group_by(subject, modality, emotion) |>
  summarise(across(all_of(sliders), mean), .groups = "drop") |>
  rename(pid = subject) |>
  pivot_longer(all_of(sliders), names_to = "slider", values_to = "value") |>
  mutate(across(c(pid, modality, emotion, slider), factor))
us_scaled <- us_long |>                                                            # D3: other DV scales
  group_by(slider) |>
  mutate(z = (value - mean(value)) / sd(value),
         range01 = (value - min(value)) / (max(value) - min(value))) |>
  ungroup() |>
  left_join(all_long |> filter(population == "us") |> select(pid, emotion, slider, discrete = value),
            by = c("pid", "emotion", "slider"))

us_variants <- list(
  "Used: raw units, MoMR = 2 people, GG"          = fit_us(us_long),
  "D1: drop both MoMR blocks (N = 48)"            = fit_us(us_drop),
  "D1: average MoMR blocks into 1 person (N = 49)" = fit_us(us_avg),
  "D3: z-scored per slider"                       = fit_us(us_scaled, dv = "z"),
  "D3: each slider rescaled to 0-1"               = fit_us(us_scaled, dv = "range01"),
  "D3: discretized 0/1/2 (Dataset S2)"            = fit_us(us_scaled, dv = "discrete"),
  "D4: Huynh-Feldt instead of GG"                 = fit_us(us_long, correction = "HF"))
imap_dfr(us_variants, \(tab, name) tibble(
  variant = name,
  `target 1: Emotion` = report_F(tab, "emotion"),
  `target 2: Emotion × Slider` = report_F(tab, "emotion:slider"),
  `target 3: Emotion × Modality` = report_F(tab, "modality:emotion"))) |>
  kable(caption = "Targets 1-3 under alternative choices (paper: 185.56 / 112.90 / 0.97)")

# --- Target 4 under alternative choices (D5, D6, D7)
comb_cont <- bind_rows(filter(s2, population == "kreung"), mutate(s1, population = "us")) |>
  pivot_longer(all_of(sliders), names_to = "slider", values_to = "value") |>
  group_by(population, slider) |>
  mutate(z = (value - mean(value)) / sd(value)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(across(c(pid, population, modality, emotion, slider), factor))
comb_alt <- all_long |>
  group_by(population, slider) |>
  mutate(z_popsd = (value - mean(value)) / sqrt(mean((value - mean(value))^2))) |>
  group_by(population, modality, slider) |>
  mutate(z_by_modality = (value - mean(value)) / sd(value)) |>
  ungroup()

comb_variants <- list(
  "Used: S2 discrete, z within population, sample SD, Type III" = fit_combined(all_long),
  "D5: Type II sums of squares"                                 = fit_combined(all_long, type = 2),
  "D6: US continuous data (S1) instead of S2 discrete"          = fit_combined(comb_cont),
  "D7: population SD (divide by n)"                             = fit_combined(comb_alt, dv = "z_popsd"),
  "D7: z within population x modality"                          = fit_combined(comb_alt, dv = "z_by_modality"),
  "D7: no z-scoring (discrete 0/1/2)"                           = fit_combined(all_long, dv = "value"))
imap_dfr(comb_variants, \(tab, name) tibble(
  variant = name, `target 4: Emotion × Sliders` = report_F(tab, "emotion:slider"))) |>
  kable(caption = "Target 4 under alternative choices (paper: F(13.68, 1791.80) = 38.22, ηp² = 0.23)")
```

- **D1. Participant IDs.** Chose to treat the two `MoMR` blocks as two participants. Why: they are
  separate blocks of five rows with different settings, and the paper's n = 25 per US group and its
  error df of 48 require 50 people. Alternatives: dropping both blocks (N = 48) or averaging them into
  one person (N = 49) shifts the df and the F values slightly. The key effect, for example, becomes
  F(4.72, 217.10) = 108.67 or F(4.76, 223.74) = 111.96 instead of 112.90 (table above). Only the
  choice I used matches.
- **D2. Exclusions.** None. The paper mentions none, and the group sizes in the data match the
  paper's n's.
- **D3. DV of the US ANOVA.** Chose raw slider values in their own units (rate 30–400 BPM, jitter
  0–99, consonance 0–37, step size and direction 0–100). The paper says only "positions of the
  sliders". Why: this is the only scale that reproduces the F values and the GG epsilons (e.g.,
  0.74 for Emotion). Alternatives: z-scored, 0–1 rescaled or discretized sliders give Emotion F of
  roughly 50–57 and a key effect of roughly 43–50 (table above), so none of the targets match. A
  caveat about the authors' choice: in raw units the rate slider's 370-point range dominates the
  sums of squares, so the US ηp² values mostly reflect rate. That affects interpretation, not
  reproducibility.
- **D4. Sphericity correction.** Chose Greenhouse–Geisser on every within-participant effect. The
  paper prints fractional df but does not name the correction. Why: GG reproduces every reported df
  exactly. Alternative: Huynh–Feldt gives larger df (table above), which do not match.
- **D5. Sums of squares.** Chose Type III, the SPSS default (the paper names no software). Why: in
  the unbalanced combined design (25/25/42/43) only Type III reproduces target 4. Type II gives
  F = `r sprintf("%.2f", filter(comb_variants[[2]], Effect == "emotion:slider")$F)` and
  ηp² = `r sprintf("%.2f", filter(comb_variants[[2]], Effect == "emotion:slider")$pes)` instead of
  38.22 and .23. For the balanced US design the two types are identical.
- **D6. US data in the combined analyses (targets 4 and 5).** Chose the authors' discretized US rows
  from Dataset S2, as given. Why: the SI says the z-scored analysis used the discrete data. My own
  nearest-value discretization agrees with S2 except at three values that sit exactly halfway
  between two levels (consonance 17 twice, step size 69), which S2 rounds down. Alternative: z-scoring
  the continuous US data (S1) instead gives
  `r report_F(comb_variants[[3]], "emotion:slider")` for target 4, which does not match.
- **D7. z-scoring.** Chose to z-score within population × slider, pooling modalities and emotions,
  with the sample SD (n − 1). The paper says "within each population" but does not give the SD
  formula. Alternatives: the population SD (n) gives
  F = `r sprintf("%.2f", filter(comb_variants[[4]], Effect == "emotion:slider")$F)`, and z-scoring
  within population × modality gives
  `r report_F(comb_variants[[5]], "emotion:slider")`. Both are close, but only the version I used is
  exact.
- **D8. Monte Carlo mean vectors.** Chose the mean of the discrete values per emotion × slider for
  each population, pooling music and movement so that each participant counts once. The paper says
  only "mean results of each experiment". Alternative: averaging the music and movement means with
  equal weight gives the same distance to three decimals.
- **D9. Monte Carlo null distribution.** Chose continuous uniform sampling and report two scales.
  The stated range (0 to 2) gives exactly half the paper's distances. A 0–4 range, which is the same
  as doubling every distance, gives the paper's null mean of 8.11 and SD of 0.97. The z-score and the
  count of close pairs do not depend on the scale, so both scales reproduce those. Alternative:
  sampling from the discrete grid {0, 1, 2} gives a null mean of
  `r sprintf("%.2f", mean(null_disc))` and SD of `r sprintf("%.2f", sd(null_disc))`, matching
  neither scale.
- **D10. Monte Carlo randomness.** Chose seed 20130102 and counted a pair as "this close" when its
  distance was ≤ the observed distance. The count is random: across 20 other seeds it ranged from
  `r min(close_counts)` to `r max(close_counts)`, always below 30 or close to it.
- **D11. US prototypes.** Chose the continuous medians from Dataset S1 with music and movement
  combined, each snapped to the nearest Table S4 value. The paper specifies this. The only open
  detail is ties: no median fell exactly halfway between two levels, and taking medians of S2's
  discrete values gives the same prototypes, so no alternative changes anything. The paper's worked
  example checks out (sad median rate = 46 BPM; sad prototype low/low/medium/low/high).
- **D12. What counts as the "Kreung result" in the prototype analysis.** Chose to average, over the
  Kreung responses for an emotion (and modality subset), each response's Euclidean distance to each
  US prototype, and to call the emotion matched if its own prototype has the smallest average. Why:
  the paper says it measured the distance of "each of the Kreung datapoints" to the prototypes.
  Alternative: the distance from the Kreung mean vector (which ranks prototypes the same way as mean

Target 5: Monte Carlo simulation
The paper represents “the mean results of each experiment as a 25-dimensional vector (five emotions × five sliders), where each dimension has a range from 0.0 to 2.0”. It then samples “the space uniformly at random, generating one-million pairs”, and compares the US–Kreung distance with the distribution of distances between the random pairs. Here the mean vectors come from the discrete data with music and movement pooled (D8), and the null distribution is continuous uniform (D9) with a fixed seed (D10).

The standardized result reproduces: on the stated 0–2 scale the observed distance is 2.12 against a null of mean 4.05 and SD 0.49, so z = 3.99. Only 44 of the 1,000,000 pairs were as close; across 20 more seeds the count ranged from 22 to 52 (mean 35.4), which is in line with “fewer than 30”. The raw distances do not match the paper: all three (observed, null mean, null SD) are exactly half the paper’s values. The paper’s numbers are what you get when every dimension spans 0–4, or equivalently when every distance is doubled (D9). The paper’s Fig. 4 axis (4 to 12) is on that doubled scale as well. Once doubled, the observed distance is 4.23 against the reported 4.24, a difference of 0.01 that I could not remove with any variant I tried (rounded means, Table S1 Kreung means, unweighted modality means).
Target 6: distance to United States prototypes
The paper derived US prototypes by “selecting the median value for each slider for each emotion (for music and movement combined) from the United States results and mapping those values to the closest Kreung setting” (D11). It then “measured the similarity of each of the Kreung datapoints to the corresponding United States prototype by calculating the Euclidean distance”. I read that as follows: for each Kreung emotion, average each response’s distance to each prototype, and call the emotion matched if its own prototype has the smallest average (D12).

All three target counts reproduce under D12. On combined data, every emotion except angry is closest to its own US prototype. Movement alone gives the same result. On music alone, happy, sad and scared match. The failures also follow the paper. Kreung angry music is closest to the US scared prototype, and angry movement is closest to happy. Kreung peaceful music is closest to the US happy prototype. One detail differs. The paper says peaceful music was “second closest to the United States ‘peaceful’ prototype”, but here the second closest is scared.
The counts are fragile. Combined peaceful beats its nearest rival by only 0.005, and movement scared by only 0.001. That fragility shows in the alternative reading: with the distance from the Kreung mean vector to each prototype, combined drops to 3 of 5 and movement to 3 of 5, because peaceful no longer matches in either. Music stays at 3 of 5.

	•	D1. Participant IDs. Chose to treat the two MoMR blocks as two participants. Why: they are separate blocks of five rows with different settings, and the paper’s n = 25 per US group and its error df of 48 require 50 people. Alternatives: dropping both blocks (N = 48) or averaging them into one person (N = 49) shifts the df and the F values slightly. The key effect, for example, becomes F(4.72, 217.10) = 108.67 or F(4.76, 223.74) = 111.96 instead of 112.90 (table above). Only the choice I used matches.
	•	D2. Exclusions. None. The paper mentions none, and the group sizes in the data match the paper’s n’s.
	•	D3. DV of the US ANOVA. Chose raw slider values in their own units (rate 30–400 BPM, jitter 0–99, consonance 0–37, step size and direction 0–100). The paper says only “positions of the sliders”. Why: this is the only scale that reproduces the F values and the GG epsilons (e.g., 0.74 for Emotion). Alternatives: z-scored, 0–1 rescaled or discretized sliders give Emotion F of roughly 50–57 and a key effect of roughly 43–50 (table above), so none of the targets match. A caveat about the authors’ choice: in raw units the rate slider’s 370-point range dominates the sums of squares, so the US ηp² values mostly reflect rate. That affects interpretation, not reproducibility.
	•	D4. Sphericity correction. Chose Greenhouse–Geisser on every within-participant effect. The paper prints fractional df but does not name the correction. Why: GG reproduces every reported df exactly. Alternative: Huynh–Feldt gives larger df (table above), which do not match.
	•	D5. Sums of squares. Chose Type III, the SPSS default (the paper names no software). Why: in the unbalanced combined design (25/25/42/43) only Type III reproduces target 4. Type II gives F = 32.23 and ηp² = 0.20 instead of 38.22 and .23. For the balanced US design the two types are identical.
	•	D6. US data in the combined analyses (targets 4 and 5). Chose the authors’ discretized US rows from Dataset S2, as given. Why: the SI says the z-scored analysis used the discrete data. My own nearest-value discretization agrees with S2 except at three values that sit exactly halfway between two levels (consonance 17 twice, step size 69), which S2 rounds down. Alternative: z-scoring the continuous US data (S1) instead gives F(13.58, 1778.70) = 40.23, p < .001, ηp² = 0.23 for target 4, which does not match.
	•	D7. z-scoring. Chose to z-score within population × slider, pooling modalities and emotions, with the sample SD (n − 1). The paper says “within each population” but does not give the SD formula. Alternatives: the population SD (n) gives F = 38.24, and z-scoring within population × modality gives F(13.70, 1794.11) = 38.21, p < .001, ηp² = 0.23. Both are close, but only the version I used is exact.
	•	D8. Monte Carlo mean vectors. Chose the mean of the discrete values per emotion × slider for each population, pooling music and movement so that each participant counts once. The paper says only “mean results of each experiment”. Alternative: averaging the music and movement means with equal weight gives the same distance to three decimals.
	•	D9. Monte Carlo null distribution. Chose continuous uniform sampling and report two scales. The stated range (0 to 2) gives exactly half the paper’s distances. A 0–4 range, which is the same as doubling every distance, gives the paper’s null mean of 8.11 and SD of 0.97. The z-score and the count of close pairs do not depend on the scale, so both scales reproduce those. Alternative: sampling from the discrete grid {0, 1, 2} gives a null mean of 5.74 and SD of 0.65, matching neither scale.
	•	D10. Monte Carlo randomness. Chose seed 20130102 and counted a pair as “this close” when its distance was ≤ the observed distance. The count is random: across 20 other seeds it ranged from 22 to 52, always below 30 or close to it.
	•	D11. US prototypes. Chose the continuous medians from Dataset S1 with music and movement combined, each snapped to the nearest Table S4 value. The paper specifies this. The only open detail is ties: no median fell exactly halfway between two levels, and taking medians of S2’s discrete values gives the same prototypes, so no alternative changes anything. The paper’s worked example checks out (sad median rate = 46 BPM; sad prototype low/low/medium/low/high).
	•	D12. What counts as the “Kreung result” in the prototype analysis. Chose to average, over the Kreung responses for an emotion (and modality subset), each response’s Euclidean distance to each US prototype, and to call the emotion matched if its own prototype has the smallest average. Why: the paper says it measured the distance of “each of the Kreung datapoints” to the prototypes. Alternative: the distance from the Kreung mean vector (which ranks prototypes the same way as mean squared distance) gives 3 of 5 combined and 3 of 5 for movement, so target 6 would not reproduce. Two matches under my choice win by less than 0.005.

Why: they are separate blocks of five rows with different settings, and the paper’s n = 25 per US group and its error df of 48 require 50 people. Alternatives: dropping both blocks (N = 48) or averaging them into one person (N = 49) shifts the df and the F values slightly. The key effect, for example, becomes F(4.72, 217.10) = 108.67 or F(4.76, 223.74) = 111.96 instead of 112.90 (table above). Only the choice I used matches.
	•	D2. Exclusions. None. The paper mentions none, and the group sizes in the data match the paper’s n’s.
	•	D3. DV of the US ANOVA. Chose raw slider values in their own units (rate 30–400 BPM, jitter 0–99, consonance 0–37, step size and direction 0–100). The paper says only “positions of the sliders”. Why: this is the only scale that reproduces the F values and the GG epsilons (e.g., 0.74 for Emotion). Alternatives: z-scored, 0–1 rescaled or discretized sliders give Emotion F of roughly 50–57 and a key effect of roughly 43–50 (table above), so none of the targets match. A caveat about the authors’ choice: in raw units the rate slider’s 370-point range dominates the sums of squares, so the US ηp² values mostly reflect rate. That affects interpretation, not reproducibility.
	•	D4. Sphericity correction. Chose Greenhouse–Geisser on every within-participant effect. The paper prints fractional df but does not name the correction. Why: GG reproduces every reported df exactly. Alternative: Huynh–Feldt gives larger df (table above), which do not match.
	•	D5. Sums of squares. Chose Type III, the SPSS default (the paper names no software). Why: in the unbalanced combined design (25/25/42/43) only Type III reproduces target 4. Type II gives F = 32.23 and ηp² = 0.20 instead of 38.22 and .23. For the balanced US design the two types are identical.
	•	D6. US data in the combined analyses (targets 4 and 5). Chose the authors’ discretized US rows from Dataset S2, as given. Why: the SI says the z-scored analysis used the discrete data. My own nearest-value discretization agrees with S2 except at three values that sit exactly halfway between two levels (consonance 17 twice, step size 69), which S2 rounds down. Alternative: z-scoring the continuous US data (S1) instead gives F(13.58, 1778.70) = 40.23, p < .001, ηp² = 0.23 for target 4, which does not match.
	•	D7. z-scoring. Chose to z-score within population × slider, pooling modalities and emotions, with the sample SD (n − 1). The paper says “within each population” but does not give the SD formula. Alternatives: the population SD (n) gives F = 38.24, and z-scoring within population × modality gives F(13.70, 1794.11) = 38.21, p < .001, ηp² = 0.23. Both are close, but only the version I used is exact.
	•	D8. Monte Carlo mean vectors. Chose the mean of the discrete values per emotion × slider for each population, pooling music and movement so that each participant counts once. The paper says only “mean results of each experiment”. Alternative: averaging the music and movement means with equal weight gives the same distance to three decimals.
	•	D9. Monte Carlo null distribution. Chose continuous uniform sampling and report two scales. The stated range (0 to 2) gives exactly half the paper’s distances. A 0–4 range, which is the same as doubling every distance, gives the paper’s null mean of 8.11 and SD of 0.97. The z-score and the count of close pairs do not depend on the scale, so both scales reproduce those. Alternative: sampling from the discrete grid {0, 1, 2} gives a null mean of 5.74 and SD of 0.65, matching neither scale.
	•	D10. Monte Carlo randomness. Chose seed 20130102 and counted a pair as “this close” when its distance was ≤ the observed distance. The count is random: across 20 other seeds it ranged from 22 to 52, always below 30 or close to it.
	•	D11. US prototypes. Chose the continuous medians from Dataset S1 with music and movement combined, each snapped to the nearest Table S4 value. The paper specifies this. The only open detail is ties: no median fell exactly halfway between two levels, and taking medians of S2’s discrete values gives the same prototypes, so no alternative changes anything. The paper’s worked example checks out (sad median rate = 46 BPM; sad prototype low/low/medium/low/high).
	•	D12. What counts as the “Kreung result” in the prototype analysis. Chose to average, over the Kreung responses for an emotion (and modality subset), each response’s Euclidean distance to each US prototype, and to call the emotion matched if its own prototype has the smallest average. Why: the paper says it measured the distance of “each of the Kreung datapoints” to the prototypes. Alternative: the distance from the Kreung mean vector (which ranks prototypes the same way as mean squared distance) gives 3 of 5 combined and 3 of 5 for movement, so target 6 would not reproduce. 542	  choice I used matches.
543	- **D2. Exclusions.** None. The paper mentions none, and the group sizes in the data match the
544	  paper's n's.
545	- **D3. DV of the US ANOVA.** Chose raw slider values in their own units (rate 30–400 BPM, jitter
546	  0–99, consonance 0–37, step size and direction 0–100). The paper says only "positions of the
547	  sliders". Why: this is the only scale that reproduces the F values and the GG epsilons (e.g.,
548	  0.74 for Emotion). Alternatives: z-scored, 0–1 rescaled or discretized sliders give Emotion F of

551	  sums of squares, so the US ηp² values mostly reflect rate. That affects interpretation, not
552	  reproducibility.

Output created: partB.html
0
The z-score reproduces up to rounding. On the stated 0–2 scale the observed distance is 2.12 against a null of mean 4.05 and SD 0.49, so z = 3.99 (paper: 3.98). The 0.01 gap comes from the observed distance, discussed below.
The count of close pairs does not clearly reproduce. With my seed, 44 of the 1,000,000 pairs were at least as close, not “fewer than 30”. The count is random: across 20 more seeds it ranged from 22 to 52 (mean 35.4), and 3 of those 20 runs came in under 30. The paper’s “fewer than 30” is therefore a possible single-run result, but a typical run gives about 35 per million. The substantive point holds under either count: the US–Kreung distance sits about 4 SDs below the mean of random pairs, and only a few dozen random pairs in a million are as close.
All three target counts reproduce under D12. On combined data, every emotion except angry is closest to its own US prototype. Movement alone gives the same result. On music alone, happy, sad and scared match. The failures also follow the paper. Kreung angry music is closest to the US scared prototype, and angry movement is closest to happy. Kreung peaceful music is closest to the US happy prototype. One detail differs. The paper says peaceful music was “second closest to the United States ‘peaceful’ prototype”, but here the second closest is scared.
The counts are fragile. Combined peaceful beats its nearest rival by only 0.0048, and movement scared by only 0.0011 (mean distances on a 0–2 grid). That fragility shows in the alternative reading: with the distance from the Kreung mean vector to each prototype, combined drops to 3 of 5 and movement to 3 of 5, because peaceful no longer matches in either. content.text:
Four of the six targets reproduce exactly (including the key effect), and the other two reproduce in substance with small discrepancies, so I think the check succeeded. Everything is in the Reproduction section of [partB.qmd](partB.qmd), and `quarto render partB.qmd` runs top to bottom without errors.

| # | Target | Result |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | US Emotion main effect | **Exact:** F(2.97, 142.44) = 185.56, ηp² = .79 |
| 2 | US Emotion × Slider (key effect) | **Exact:** F(4.81, 230.73) = 112.90, ηp² = .70 |
| 3 | US Emotion × Modality | **Exact:** F(2.97, 142.44) = 0.97, p = .407, ηp² = .02 |
| 4 | Combined US + Kreung Emotion × Sliders | **Exact:** F(13.68, 1791.80) = 38.22, ηp² = .23. The other 9 effects in that paragraph match too. |
| 5 | Monte Carlo distance | **Partly.** z = 3.99 vs 3.98. On the 0–2 range the paper states, every distance comes out exactly half the paper's. The paper's numbers match a 0–4 range, and doubled, the US–Kreung distance is 4.23 vs 4.24. The paper says fewer than 30 of a million random pairs were as close. My seed gives 44, and 20 other seeds give 22–52 (mean 35), so "fewer than 30" looks like a lucky draw. |
| 6 | Kreung emotions closest to the matching US prototype | **Reproduced, but fragile.** Combined 4 of 5 (not angry), movement 4 of 5, music 3 of 5 (happy, sad, scared), as in the paper. Two of those matches win by less than 0.005, and under the other reasonable reading combined and movement drop to 3 of 5. |

Three things only the data revealed, and that you may want in your verdict:

- **Duplicated participant label.** `MoMR` labels two separate blocks of five rows. The paper's numbers only come out if they're treated as two people, which gives the 50 US participants the paper reports.
- **Raw slider units.** The US ANOVA only matches on raw slider values, where the rate slider (30–400) dominates. Leaving rate out drops the Emotion effect from ηp² = .79 to .42. That affects how to read the result, not whether it reproduces.
- **Typos in SI Table S2.** Two US "Size" cells look wrong: peaceful has its sign flipped, and sad is printed as −0.49 where the data give −0.41. Neither is a target.

**Analysis decisions:** all 12 are listed in the qmd with what I chose and why. Where an alternative changes a result, both versions are shown. The ones that decide whether a target matches:

- **US ANOVA (targets 1–3):** raw slider units, `MoMR` as two people, Greenhouse–Geisser correction.
- **Combined ANOVA (target 4):** Type III sums of squares, and the authors' discretized US data z-scored within each population.
- **Monte Carlo (target 5):** which range to sample from (0–2 vs 0–4).
- **Prototypes (target 6):** averaging each Kreung response's distance to the prototypes, rather than taking the distance from the Kreung average.

Every package I needed was already installed. The data files and the other sections are unchanged, "Checker's verdict" is still blank, and nothing is committed.

1	---
2	title: "Reproducibility check: Sievers et al. (2013)"
3	author: "Nick Madibekov"
4	date: today
5	format:
6	  html:
7	    toc: true
8	execute:
9	  echo: true
10	  warning: false
11	  message: false
12	---
13	
14	## Article
15	
16	- Citation and DOI: Sievers, B., Polansky, L., Casey, M., & Wheatley, T. (2013). Music and
17	  movement share a dynamic structure that supports universal expressions of emotion.
18	  *Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 110*(1), 70–75.
19	  <https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1209023110>
20	- Data/materials repository URL: no separate repository; the data are the paper's supporting
21	  information on PNAS (<https://www.pnas.org/lookup/suppl/doi:10.1073/pnas.1209023110/-/DCSupplemental>),
22	  mirrored on PubMed Central (<https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3538264/>): Datasets S1–S2
23	  (`.xlsx`), the SI text (PDF), and the audio and video stimuli.
24	- Part A (known case) or Part B (a classmate's project paper): Part B
25	- Part B only: the classmate's project repo, and which target outcome is its key effect:
26	  <https://github.com/psych251/sievers2012>. Key effect: **row 2**, the Emotion × Slider
27	  interaction in the United States experiment (ηp² = .70).
28	
29	## Target outcomes
30	
31	Written **before** opening the data. Quote each from the paper. In Part B, one of these must
32	be the project's key effect.
33	
34	Rows 1–3 come from the United States experiment (*n* = 50; music *n* = 25, movement
35	*n* = 25), rows 4–6 from the combined United States + Kreung analyses (Kreung music *n* = 42,
36	movement *n* = 43). Together they cover the abstract's claims: each emotion has a unique
37	combination of features (rows 2, 4), the same combination works in music and movement (row 3), and
38	the structure holds across cultures (rows 5, 6).
39	
40	| # | Target outcome (quoted) | Paper value(s) |
41	|---|---|---|
42	| 1 | US experiment, multiway ANOVA: "Emotion had the largest main effect on slider position [F(2.97, 142.44) = 185.56, P < 0.001, partial η2 = 0.79]" | *F*(2.97, 142.44) = 185.56, *p* < .001, ηp² = .79 |
43	| 2 | **Key effect.** US experiment: "an Emotion × Slider interaction indicating each emotion required different slider settings [F(4.81, 230.73) = 112.90, P < 0.001; partial η2 = 0.70]" | *F*(4.81, 230.73) = 112.90, *p* < .001, ηp² = .70 |
44	| 3 | US experiment: modality "did not interact with Emotion [Emotion × Modality: F(2.97, 142.44) = 0.97, P > 0.4; partial η2 = 0.02]" | *F*(2.97, 142.44) = 0.97, *p* > .4, ηp² = .02 |
45	| 4 | Combined US + Kreung ANOVA on z-scored sliders: "an Emotion × Sliders interaction, indicating each emotion was expressed by different slider settings [F(13.68, 1791.80) = 38.22, P < 0.001; partial η2 = 0.23]" | *F*(13.68, 1791.80) = 38.22, *p* < .001, ηp² = .23 |
46	| 5 | Monte Carlo simulation: "The distance between the Kreung and United States mean result vectors was 4.24, which was 3.98 SDs away from the mean"; null distribution "(mean = 8.11, SD = 0.97)"; "fewer than 30 pairs were this close together" out of one million | distance = 4.24; null mean = 8.11, SD = 0.97; *z* = 3.98; < 30 / 1,000,000 pairs |
47	| 6 | Prototype analysis: "For every emotion except 'angry,'" Kreung results (music and movement combined) were closer to the matching US prototype than to any other; the same held for movement alone; for music alone, "three of the five emotions (happy, sad, and scared)" | combined: 4 of 5 (not angry); movement: 4 of 5; music: 3 of 5 (happy, sad, scared) |
48	
49	## Materials inventory
50	
51	| Item | Available? | Notes |
52	|---|---|---|
53	| Raw data | Yes | Each participant's final slider settings, one row per participant × emotion, from the SI on PubMed Central. Dataset S1 (`partB/data/Dataset_S01.xlsx`): United States, continuous values, 250 rows. Dataset S2 (`partB/data/Dataset_S02.xlsx`): all participants (United States and Kreung), discrete values 0/1/2, 675 rows. No slider-movement logs or demographics. |
54	| Processed data | Partial | According to the SI, the United States rows of Dataset S2 are Dataset S1 discretized to three levels (cut-points in SI Table S4), to match the Kreung program's three positions. Group means are in SI Table S1 (raw) and Table S2 (z-scored). There are no participant-level z-scored data. |
55	| Codebook / variable descriptions | Partial | No codebook file. Column meanings come from the Methods and SI Table S1: `bpm` = rate (30–400), `jitter` (0–99), `consonance` = consonance / visual spikiness (0–37), `bigsmall` = step size (0–100), `updown` = direction (0–100); `task modality` = `music` or `motion` (movement); `population` = `us` or `kreung`. The first column is an unnamed row index. |
56	| Analysis code | No | None shared. The paper names the analyses (repeated-measures ANOVA with Greenhouse–Geisser correction, a Monte Carlo simulation, distances to emotion prototypes) but not the software or every setting. The stimulus program (Max/MSP, Processing) is not analysis code. |
57	| Preregistration | No | Not preregistered (published 2012). |
58	
59	## Reproduction
60	
61	The agent's work, under your direction. Keep all code visible.
62	
63	Everything below uses only `partB/data/Dataset_S01.xlsx` and `partB/data/Dataset_S02.xlsx`,
64	which are read but never modified. Wherever the paper and SI leave a choice open it is tagged
65	**D1–D12**, and each choice is explained, with its alternatives, under
66	[Analysis decisions](#analysis-decisions). The [summary table](#summary-table) at the end gives
67	one row per target.
68	
69	```{r}
70	#| label: setup
71	library(tidyverse)
72	library(readxl)   # read the .xlsx datasets
73	library(rstatix)  # mixed ANOVA; the GG / HF corrections come from car::Anova
74	library(knitr)    # kable() tables
75	
76	sliders  <- c("bpm", "jitter", "consonance", "bigsmall", "updown")
77	emotions <- c("angry", "happy", "peaceful", "sad", "scared")
78	# Symbols inside R strings are written as HTML entities (η, ², ×) so the tables
79	# render correctly whatever the R session's locale.
80	
81	# Mixed ANOVA with Emotion x Slider within participants.
82	# US experiment: Modality between. Combined analysis: Population x Modality between.
83	# Returns a tibble whose DFn / DFd are the sphericity-corrected df.
84	fit_us <- function(d, dv = "value", correction = "GG", type = 3) {
85	  res <- anova_test(data = d, dv = !!dv, wid = pid, between = modality,
86	                    within = c(emotion, slider), effect.size = "pes", type = type)
87	  as_tibble(as.data.frame(get_anova_table(res, correction = correction)))
88	}
89	fit_combined <- function(d, dv = "z", correction = "GG", type = 3) {
90	  res <- anova_test(data = d, dv = !!dv, wid = pid, between = c(population, modality),
91	                    within = c(emotion, slider), effect.size = "pes", type = type)
92	  as_tibble(as.data.frame(get_anova_table(res, correction = correction)))
93	}
94	
95	# One effect as "F(df1, df2) = F, p, partial eta^2", formatted like the paper
96	report_F <- function(tab, effect) {
97	  r  <- filter(tab, Effect == effect)
98	  df <- function(x) if (x == round(x)) sprintf("%d", as.integer(x)) else sprintf("%.2f", x)
99	  f  <- if (r$F < .001) "< 0.001" else if (r$F < 1) sprintf("= %.3f", r$F) else sprintf("= %.2f", r$F)
100	  p  <- if (r$p < .001) "< .001" else sprintf("= %.3f", r$p)
101	  sprintf("F(%s, %s) %s, p %s, ηp² = %.2f", df(r$DFn), df(r$DFd), f, p, r$pes)
102	}
103	```
104	
105	### Data
106	
107	```{r}
108	#| label: load
109	# Column 1 is an unnamed row index; keep it as `row`.
110	s1_raw <- read_excel("partB/data/Dataset_S01.xlsx", .name_repair = "unique_quiet") |>
111	  rename(row = 1, modality = `task modality`)
112	s2_raw <- read_excel("partB/data/Dataset_S02.xlsx", .name_repair = "unique_quiet") |>
113	  rename(row = 1, modality = `task modality`)
114	
115	dim(s1_raw)
116	dim(s2_raw)
117	count(s2_raw, population, modality)
118	
119	# Each subject label should have 5 rows (one per emotion). One label has 10:
120	s1_raw |> count(subject) |> filter(n != 5)
121	s1_raw |> filter(subject == "MoMR") |> select(row, subject, emotion, modality, all_of(sliders))
122	```
123	
124	The label `MoMR` appears in two separate blocks of five rows (rows 221–225 and 236–240, with two
125	other participants in between), and the two blocks hold different settings. The paper reports 25
126	movement participants, and its error df (48 = 50 − 2) needs 50 US participants, but the file has only

230	### Targets 1–3: United States ANOVA
231	
232	The paper analyzed "the positions of the sliders for each modality … and each emotion … using
233	multiway ANOVA". I fit a mixed ANOVA with Emotion (5) × Slider (5) within participants and Modality
234	(music vs. movement) between participants. The dependent variable is the raw slider value in its own
235	units (**D3**). Every within-participant effect gets the Greenhouse–Geisser correction (**D4**),
236	and sums of squares are Type III (**D5**). The US design is balanced, so Type II gives the same
237	result.

301	### Target 5: Monte Carlo simulation
302	
303	The paper represents "the mean results of each experiment as a 25-dimensional vector (five
304	emotions × five sliders), where each dimension has a range from 0.0 to 2.0". It then samples "the
305	space uniformly at random, generating one-million pairs", and compares the US–Kreung distance with
306	the distribution of distances between the random pairs. Here the mean vectors come from the
307	discrete data with music and movement pooled (**D8**), and the null distribution is continuous
308	uniform (**D9**) with a fixed seed (**D10**).
309	
310	```{r}
311	#| label: analysis-montecarlo
312	# 25-d mean vectors (5 emotions x 5 sliders) of the discrete data, music and movement pooled
313	mean_vecs <- s2 |>
314	  group_by(population, emotion) |>
315	  summarise(across(all_of(sliders), mean), .groups = "drop")
316	v_us     <- mean_vecs |> filter(population == "us")     |> select(all_of(sliders)) |> as.matrix()
317	v_kreung <- mean_vecs |> filter(population == "kreung") |> select(all_of(sliders)) |> as.matrix()
318	d_obs <- sqrt(sum((v_us - v_kreung)^2))
319	d_obs
320	
321	# Null: distances between pairs of 25-d vectors drawn uniformly from [0, width]^25.
322	# Summing squared differences one dimension at a time keeps memory small.
323	sim_distances <- function(n_pairs, width) {
324	  d2 <- numeric(n_pairs)
325	  for (j in 1:25) d2 <- d2 + (runif(n_pairs, 0, width) - runif(n_pairs, 0, width))^2
326	  sqrt(d2)
327	}
328	set.seed(20130102)
329	null_02 <- sim_distances(1e6, width = 2)  # the range the paper states (0.0 to 2.0)
330	null_04 <- 2 * null_02                    # a [0, 4] draw is exactly 2 x a [0, 2] draw
331	
332	mc_tab <- tibble(
333	  version  = c("Paper", "Stated range, 0 to 2", "Doubled: 0 to 4 (every distance × 2)"),
334	  observed = c(4.24, d_obs, 2 * d_obs),
335	  null_mean = c(8.11, mean(null_02), mean(null_04)),
336	  null_sd  = c(0.97, sd(null_02), sd(null_04)),
337	  z        = c(3.98, (mean(null_02) - d_obs) / sd(null_02), (mean(null_04) - 2 * d_obs) / sd(null_04)),
338	  pairs_at_least_as_close = c("fewer than 30", sum(null_02 <= d_obs), sum(null_04 <= 2 * d_obs)))
339	mc_tab |> kable(digits = 2, caption = "Monte Carlo: paper vs. reproduced (1,000,000 random pairs)")
340	
341	# The count of close pairs is random: repeat with 20 more seeds
342	set.seed(1)
343	close_counts <- replicate(20, sum(sim_distances(1e6, width = 2) <= d_obs))
344	summary(close_counts)
345	
346	# Alternative null (D9): discrete uniform on {0, 1, 2}
347	set.seed(2)
348	null_disc <- sqrt(rowSums((matrix(sample(0:2, 25 * 1e5, TRUE), ncol = 25) -
349	                           matrix(sample(0:2, 25 * 1e5, TRUE), ncol = 25))^2))
350	c(mean = mean(null_disc), sd = sd(null_disc))
351	
352	ggplot(tibble(distance = null_04), aes(distance)) +
353	  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.1, fill = "grey70", colour = "grey40") +
354	  geom_vline(xintercept = 2 * d_obs, linewidth = 1) +
355	  annotate("text", x = 2 * d_obs, y = Inf, label = sprintf("%.2f", 2 * d_obs), vjust = 1.5, hjust = -0.1) +
356	  labs(title = "Null distribution on the doubled (0-4) scale, as in the paper's Fig. 4",
357	       x = "Distance", y = "Frequency") +
358	  theme_minimal()
359	```
360	
361	The *z*-score reproduces up to rounding. On the stated 0–2 scale the observed distance is
362	`r sprintf("%.2f", d_obs)` against a null of mean `r sprintf("%.2f", mean(null_02))` and SD
363	`r sprintf("%.2f", sd(null_02))`, so *z* = `r sprintf("%.2f", (mean(null_02) - d_obs) / sd(null_02))`
364	(paper: 3.98). The 0.01 gap comes from the observed distance, discussed below.
365	
366	The count of close pairs does not clearly reproduce. With my seed, `r sum(null_02 <= d_obs)` of the
367	1,000,000 pairs were at least as close, not "fewer than 30". The count is random: across 20 more
368	seeds it ranged from `r min(close_counts)` to `r max(close_counts)` (mean
369	`r sprintf("%.1f", mean(close_counts))`), and `r sum(close_counts < 30)` of those 20 runs came in
370	under 30. The paper's "fewer than 30" is therefore a possible single-run result, but a typical run
371	gives about `r round(mean(close_counts))` per million. The substantive point holds under either
372	count: the US–Kreung distance sits about 4 SDs below the mean of random pairs, and only a few dozen
373	random pairs in a million are as close.
374	
375	The raw distances do not match the paper. All three (observed, null mean, null SD) are exactly half
376	the paper's values. The paper's numbers are what you get when every dimension spans 0–4, or
377	equivalently when every distance is doubled (**D9**), and the axis of the paper's Fig. 4 (4 to 12)
378	is on that doubled scale too. Once doubled, the observed distance is `r sprintf("%.2f", 2 * d_obs)`
379	against the reported 4.24. I could not close that 0.01 gap with any variant I tried (means rounded
380	to two decimals, the Table S1 Kreung means, unweighted modality means).

382	### Target 6: distance to United States prototypes
383	
384	The paper derived US prototypes by "selecting the median value for each slider for each emotion
385	(for music and movement combined) from the United States results and mapping those values to the
386	closest Kreung setting" (**D11**). It then "measured the similarity of each of the Kreung
387	datapoints to the corresponding United States prototype by calculating the Euclidean distance". I
388	read that as follows: for each Kreung emotion, average each response's distance to each prototype,
389	and call the emotion matched if its own prototype has the smallest average (**D12**).
390	
391	```{r}
392	#| label: analysis-prototypes
393	# US prototypes: median of the continuous US data per emotion x slider (music + movement),
394	# snapped to the nearest Kreung setting in Table S4 (0 = low, 1 = medium, 2 = high)
395	us_medians <- s1 |> group_by(emotion) |> summarise(across(all_of(sliders), median))
396	prototypes <- us_medians |>
397	  mutate(across(all_of(sliders), \(x) nearest_level(x, s4_levels[[cur_column()]])))
398	us_medians |> kable(caption = "US medians (continuous units)")
399	prototypes |> kable(caption = "US prototypes (0 = low, 1 = medium, 2 = high)")
400	# Paper: sad median rate = 46 BPM; sad prototype = low rate, low jitter, medium consonance,
401	# low step size, high (downward) direction
402	stopifnot(us_medians$bpm[us_medians$emotion == "sad"] == 46,
403	          all(prototypes[prototypes$emotion == "sad", sliders] == c(0, 0, 1, 0, 2)),
404	          !anyNA(prototypes))
405	
406	proto_mat <- prototypes |> select(all_of(sliders)) |> as.matrix()
407	rownames(proto_mat) <- prototypes$emotion
408	# Euclidean distance from each row of X (5 slider values) to each of the 5 prototypes
409	dist_to_protos <- function(X) t(apply(X, 1, function(v) sqrt(colSums((t(proto_mat) - v)^2))))
410	
411	kreung  <- filter(s2, population == "kreung")
412	subsets <- list(combined = c("music", "motion"), music = "music", movement = "motion")
413	
414	# method "mean_of_distances": average over responses of response-to-prototype distance (D12)
415	# method "distance_of_mean":  distance from the Kreung mean vector to each prototype (alternative)
416	proto_results <- function(method) {
417	  imap_dfr(subsets, function(mods, subset_name) {
418	    map_dfr(emotions, function(e) {
419	      X <- kreung |> filter(modality %in% mods, emotion == e) |> select(all_of(sliders)) |> as.matrix()
420	      d <- if (method == "mean_of_distances") colMeans(dist_to_protos(X))
421	           else dist_to_protos(matrix(colMeans(X), nrow = 1))[1, ]
422	      names(d) <- rownames(proto_mat)
423	      ord <- sort(d)
424	      tibble(subset = subset_name, kreung_emotion = e, closest = names(ord)[1], second = names(ord)[2],
425	             dist_own = d[[e]], dist_nearest_other = min(d[names(d) != e]))
426	    })
427	  }) |> mutate(matched = closest == kreung_emotion, margin = dist_nearest_other - dist_own)
428	}
429	proto_counts <- function(res) {
430	  res |>
431	    mutate(subset = factor(subset, levels = names(subsets))) |>
432	    group_by(subset) |>
433	    summarise(n_matched = sum(matched),
434	              matched_emotions = paste(kreung_emotion[matched], collapse = ", "),
435	              unmatched_emotions = paste(kreung_emotion[!matched], collapse = ", "))
436	}
437	
438	proto_main <- proto_results("mean_of_distances")
439	proto_main |> kable(digits = 3, caption = "Mean distance from Kreung responses to US prototypes (D12)")
440	proto_main_counts <- proto_counts(proto_main)
441	proto_main_counts |>
442	  mutate(paper = c("4 of 5 (all but angry)", "3 of 5 (happy, sad, scared)", "4 of 5 (all but angry)")) |>
443	  kable(caption = "Kreung emotions closest to the matching US prototype: reproduced vs. paper")
444	
445	# Alternative (D12): distance from the Kreung mean vector
446	proto_alt <- proto_results("distance_of_mean")
447	proto_alt_counts <- proto_counts(proto_alt)
448	proto_alt_counts |> kable(caption = "Alternative: distance from the Kreung mean vector")
449	```
450	
451	```{r}
452	#| label: prototype-details
453	#| include: false
454	pm <- function(sub, emo, col) filter(proto_main, subset == sub, kreung_emotion == emo)[[col]]
455	```
456	
457	All three target counts reproduce under D12. On combined data, every emotion except angry is closest
458	to its own US prototype. Movement alone gives the same result. On music alone, happy, sad and
459	scared match. The failures also follow the paper. Kreung angry music is closest to the US
460	`r pm("music", "angry", "closest")` prototype, and angry movement is closest to
461	`r pm("movement", "angry", "closest")`. Kreung peaceful music is closest to the US
462	`r pm("music", "peaceful", "closest")` prototype. One detail differs. The paper says peaceful music
463	was "second closest to the United States 'peaceful' prototype", but here the second closest is
464	`r pm("music", "peaceful", "second")`.
465	
466	The counts are fragile. Combined peaceful beats its nearest rival by only
467	`r sprintf("%.4f", pm("combined", "peaceful", "margin"))`, and movement scared by only
468	`r sprintf("%.4f", pm("movement", "scared", "margin"))` (mean distances on a 0–2 grid). That fragility shows in the alternative
469	reading: with the distance from the Kreung mean vector to each prototype, combined drops to
470	`r proto_alt_counts$n_matched[1]` of 5 and movement to `r proto_alt_counts$n_matched[3]` of 5,
471	because peaceful no longer matches in either. Music stays at `r proto_alt_counts$n_matched[2]` of 5.

473	### Analysis decisions {#analysis-decisions}

476	happens under a reasonable alternative.
477	
478	```{r}

481	us_drop <- us_long |> filter(!str_detect(pid, "^MoMR")) |> droplevels()           # D1: drop both MoMR blocks
482	us_avg  <- s1 |>                                                                   # D1: MoMR as one person (average)
483	  group_by(subject, modality, emotion) |>
484	  summarise(across(all_of(sliders), mean), .groups = "drop") |>
485	  rename(pid = subject) |>
486	  pivot_longer(all_of(sliders), names_to = "slider", values_to = "value") |>
487	  mutate(across(c(pid, modality, emotion, slider), factor))
488	us_scaled <- us_long |>                                                            # D3: other DV scales
489	  group_by(slider) |>
490	  mutate(z = (value - mean(value)) / sd(value),
491	         range01 = (value - min(value)) / (max(value) - min(value))) |>
492	  ungroup() |>
493	  left_join(all_long |> filter(population == "us") |> select(pid, emotion, slider, discrete = value),
494	            by = c("pid", "emotion", "slider"))
495	
496	us_variants <- list(
497	  "Used: raw units, MoMR = 2 people, GG"          = fit_us(us_long),
498	  "D1: drop both MoMR blocks (N = 48)"            = fit_us(us_drop),
499	  "D1: average MoMR blocks into 1 person (N = 49)" = fit_us(us_avg),
500	  "D3: z-scored per slider"                       = fit_us(us_scaled, dv = "z"),
501	  "D3: each slider rescaled to 0-1"               = fit_us(us_scaled, dv = "range01"),
502	  "D3: discretized 0/1/2 (Dataset S2)"            = fit_us(us_scaled, dv = "discrete"),
503	  "D4: Huynh-Feldt instead of GG"                 = fit_us(us_long, correction = "HF"),
504	  "Caveat check for D3: raw units, rate slider left out (4 sliders)" =
505	    fit_us(us_long |> filter(slider != "bpm") |> droplevels()))
506	imap_dfr(us_variants, \(tab, name) tibble(
507	  variant = name,
508	  `target 1: Emotion` = report_F(tab, "emotion"),
509	  `target 2: Emotion × Slider` = report_F(tab, "emotion:slider"),
510	  `target 3: Emotion × Modality` = report_F(tab, "modality:emotion"))) |>
511	  kable(caption = "Targets 1-3 under alternative choices (paper: 185.56 / 112.90 / 0.97)")
512	
513	# --- Target 4 under alternative choices (D5, D6, D7)
514	comb_cont <- bind_rows(filter(s2, population == "kreung"), mutate(s1, population = "us")) |>
515	  pivot_longer(all_of(sliders), names_to = "slider", values_to = "value") |>
516	  group_by(population, slider) |>
517	  mutate(z = (value - mean(value)) / sd(value)) |>
518	  ungroup() |>
519	  mutate(across(c(pid, population, modality, emotion, slider), factor))
520	comb_alt <- all_long |>
521	  group_by(population, slider) |>
522	  mutate(z_popsd = (value - mean(value)) / sqrt(mean((value - mean(value))^2))) |>
523	  group_by(population, modality, slider) |>
524	  mutate(z_by_modality = (value - mean(value)) / sd(value)) |>
525	  ungroup()
526	
527	comb_variants <- list(
528	  "Used: S2 discrete, z within population, sample SD, Type III" = fit_combined(all_long),
529	  "D5: Type II sums of squares"                                 = fit_combined(all_long, type = 2),
530	  "D6: US continuous data (S1) instead of S2 discrete"          = fit_combined(comb_cont),
531	  "D7: population SD (divide by n)"                             = fit_combined(comb_alt, dv = "z_popsd"),
532	  "D7: z within population x modality"                          = fit_combined(comb_alt, dv = "z_by_modality"),
533	  "D7: no z-scoring (discrete 0/1/2)"                           = fit_combined(all_long, dv = "value"))
534	imap_dfr(comb_variants, \(tab, name) tibble(
535	  variant = name, `target 4: Emotion × Sliders` = report_F(tab, "emotion:slider"))) |>
536	  kable(caption = "Target 4 under alternative choices (paper: F(13.68, 1791.80) = 38.22, ηp² = 0.23)")
537	```
538	
539	- **D1. Participant IDs.** Chose to treat the two `MoMR` blocks as two participants. Why: they are
540	  separate blocks of five rows with different settings, and the paper's n = 25 per US group and its
541	  error df of 48 require 50 people. Alternatives: dropping both blocks (N = 48) or averaging them into
542	  one person (N = 49) shifts the df and the F values slightly. The key effect, for example, becomes
543	  `r report_F(us_variants[[2]], "emotion:slider")` or
544	  `r report_F(us_variants[[3]], "emotion:slider")` instead of F(4.81, 230.73) = 112.90 (table above).
545	  Only the choice I used matches.
546	- **D2. Exclusions.** None. The paper mentions none, and the group sizes in the data match the
547	  paper's n's.
548	- **D3. DV of the US ANOVA.** Chose raw slider values in their own units (rate 30–400 BPM, jitter
549	  0–99, consonance 0–37, step size and direction 0–100). The paper says only "positions of the
550	  sliders". Why: this is the only scale that reproduces the F values and the GG epsilons (e.g.,
551	  0.74 for Emotion). Alternatives: z-scored, 0–1 rescaled or discretized sliders give an Emotion F
552	  of roughly 54–57 and a key effect of roughly 43–50 (table above), so none of the targets match. A
553	  caveat about the authors' choice: in raw units the rate slider (range 30–400) dominates the sums
554	  of squares. With rate left out, the Emotion effect drops to
555	  `r report_F(us_variants[[8]], "emotion")` (last row of the table above). This bears on how to
556	  interpret the US ηp² values, not on whether they reproduce.
557	- **D4. Sphericity correction.** Chose Greenhouse–Geisser on every within-participant effect. The
558	  paper prints fractional df but does not name the correction. Why: GG reproduces every reported df
559	  exactly. Alternative: Huynh–Feldt gives larger df (table above), which do not match.
560	- **D5. Sums of squares.** Chose Type III, the SPSS default (the paper names no software). Why: in
561	  the unbalanced combined design (25/25/42/43) only Type III reproduces target 4. Type II gives
562	  F = `r sprintf("%.2f", filter(comb_variants[[2]], Effect == "emotion:slider")$F)` and
563	  ηp² = `r sprintf("%.2f", filter(comb_variants[[2]], Effect == "emotion:slider")$pes)` instead of
564	  38.22 and .23. For the balanced US design the two types are identical.
565	- **D6. US data in the combined analyses (targets 4 and 5).** Chose the authors' discretized US rows
566	  from Dataset S2, as given. Why: the SI says the z-scored analysis used the discrete data. My own
567	  nearest-value discretization agrees with S2 except at three values that sit exactly halfway
568	  between two levels (consonance 17 twice, step size 69), which S2 rounds down. Alternative: z-scoring
569	  the continuous US data (S1) instead gives
570	  `r report_F(comb_variants[[3]], "emotion:slider")` for target 4, which does not match.
571	- **D7. z-scoring.** Chose to z-score within population × slider, pooling modalities and emotions,
572	  with the sample SD (n − 1). The paper says "within each population" but does not give the SD
573	  formula. Alternatives: the population SD (n) gives
574	  F = `r sprintf("%.2f", filter(comb_variants[[4]], Effect == "emotion:slider")$F)`, and z-scoring
575	  within population × modality gives
576	  `r report_F(comb_variants[[5]], "emotion:slider")`. Both are close, but only the version I used is
577	  exact.
578	- **D8. Monte Carlo mean vectors.** Chose the mean of the discrete values per emotion × slider for
579	  each population, pooling music and movement so that each participant counts once. The paper says
580	  only "mean results of each experiment". Alternative: averaging the music and movement means with
581	  equal weight gives the same distance to three decimals.
582	- **D9. Monte Carlo null distribution.** Chose continuous uniform sampling and report two scales.
583	  The stated range (0 to 2) gives exactly half the paper's distances. A 0–4 range, which is the same
584	  as doubling every distance, gives the paper's null mean of 8.11 and SD of 0.97. The z-score and the
585	  count of close pairs do not depend on the scale, so the two scales give identical values for
586	  those. Alternative:
587	  sampling from the discrete grid {0, 1, 2} gives a null mean of
588	  `r sprintf("%.2f", mean(null_disc))` and SD of `r sprintf("%.2f", sd(null_disc))`, matching
589	  neither scale.
590	- **D10. Monte Carlo randomness.** Chose seed 20130102 and counted a pair as "this close" when its
591	  distance was ≤ the observed distance. I did not search for a seed that matches the paper. The
592	  count is random: my seed gives `r sum(null_02 <= d_obs)`, and across 20 other seeds the count
593	  ranged from `r min(close_counts)` to `r max(close_counts)` (`r sum(close_counts < 30)` of 20 below
594	  30). The paper's "fewer than 30" is consistent with one lucky draw.
595	- **D11. US prototypes.** Chose the continuous medians from Dataset S1 with music and movement
596	  combined, each snapped to the nearest Table S4 value. The paper specifies this. The only open
597	  detail is ties: no median fell exactly halfway between two levels, and taking medians of S2's
598	  discrete values gives the same prototypes, so no alternative changes anything. The paper's worked
599	  example checks out (sad median rate = 46 BPM; sad prototype low/low/medium/low/high).
600	- **D12. What counts as the "Kreung result" in the prototype analysis.** Chose to average, over the
601	  Kreung responses for an emotion (and modality subset), each response's Euclidean distance to each
602	  US prototype, and to call the emotion matched if its own prototype has the smallest average. Why:
603	  the paper says it measured the distance of "each of the Kreung datapoints" to the prototypes.
604	  Alternative: the distance from the Kreung mean vector (which ranks prototypes the same way as mean
605	  squared distance) gives `r proto_alt_counts$n_matched[1]` of 5 combined and
606	  `r proto_alt_counts$n_matched[3]` of 5 for movement, so target 6 would not reproduce. Two matches
607	  under my choice win by less than 0.005.
608	
609	### Summary table {#summary-table}
610	
611	```{r}
612	#| label: summary-table
613	mc <- function(x) sprintf("%.2f", x)
614	tibble(
615	  `#` = 1:6,
616	  target = c("US: Emotion main effect", "US: Emotion × Slider (key effect)", "US: Emotion × Modality",
617	             "US + Kreung: Emotion × Sliders", "Monte Carlo: US vs. Kreung distance",
618	             "Kreung closest to matching US prototype"),
619	  `paper value(s)` = c(
620	    "F(2.97, 142.44) = 185.56, p < .001, ηp² = .79",
621	    "F(4.81, 230.73) = 112.90, p < .001, ηp² = .70",
622	    "F(2.97, 142.44) = 0.97, p > .4, ηp² = .02",
623	    "F(13.68, 1791.80) = 38.22, p < .001, ηp² = .23",
624	    "distance = 4.24; null M = 8.11, SD = 0.97; z = 3.98; < 30 of 1,000,000 pairs as close",
625	    "combined: 4 of 5 (not angry); movement: 4 of 5; music: 3 of 5 (happy, sad, scared)"),
626	  `reproduced value(s)` = c(
627	    report_F(us_tab, "emotion"),
628	    report_F(us_tab, "emotion:slider"),
629	    report_F(us_tab, "modality:emotion"),
630	    report_F(comb_tab, "emotion:slider"),
631	    sprintf("0-2 scale: distance = %s; null M = %s, SD = %s; z = %s; %d of 1,000,000 pairs. Doubled (0-4): distance = %s; null M = %s, SD = %s",
632	            mc(d_obs), mc(mean(null_02)), mc(sd(null_02)), mc((mean(null_02) - d_obs) / sd(null_02)),
633	            sum(null_02 <= d_obs), mc(2 * d_obs), mc(mean(null_04)), mc(sd(null_04))),
634	    with(proto_main_counts, sprintf("combined: %d of 5 (not %s); movement: %d of 5 (not %s); music: %d of 5 (%s)",
635	                                    n_matched[1], unmatched_emotions[1], n_matched[3], unmatched_emotions[3],
636	                                    n_matched[2], matched_emotions[2]))),
637	  note = c(
638	    "Exact. Requires raw slider units (D3), MoMR as two participants (D1), GG (D4).",
639	    "Exact, same requirements as row 1.",
640	    "Exact (p = .407).",
641	    "Exact. Requires Type III SS (D5), S2 discrete US data (D6), z within population with sample SD (D7). The other 9 effects in the paragraph also match (Emotion × Modality p = .027 vs. printed .02).",
642	    sprintf("z reproduces to rounding (%s vs. 3.98, because the observed distance is %s vs. 4.24 after doubling). Every distance on the stated 0-2 scale is exactly half the paper's; the paper's numbers match a 0-4 range (D9). The close-pair count is random: %d with my seed, %d-%d across 20 other seeds (mean %.0f), so 'fewer than 30' is a possible but below-typical draw (D10).",
643	            mc((mean(null_02) - d_obs) / sd(null_02)), mc(2 * d_obs),
644	            sum(null_02 <= d_obs), min(close_counts), max(close_counts), mean(close_counts)),
645	    "Reproduced with the mean of per-response distances (D12), including which emotions fail. Fragile: two matches win by < .005, and the Kreung-mean-vector reading gives 3 of 5 combined and 3 of 5 movement. Peaceful music's second-closest prototype is scared, not peaceful as the paper says.")
646	) |> kable(caption = "Summary: one row per target outcome")
647	```
648	
649	## Checker's verdict
650	
651	Filled in by you, not the agent.
652	
653	| # | Paper value | Reproduced value | Verdict (exact / minor / major / not reproducible) | Reason for discrepancy |
654	|---|---|---|---|---|
655	| 1 | *F*(2.97, 142.44) = 185.56, *p* < .001, ηp² = .79 | *F*(2.97, 142.44) = 185.56, *p* < .001, ηp² = .79 | exact | none, it takes 3 choices the paper doesn't state: raw slider units as the DV, the label `MoMR` split into two participants, and the Greenhouse–Geisser correction |
656	| 2 | **Key effect.** *F*(4.81, 230.73) = 112.90, *p* < .001, ηp² = .70 | *F*(4.81, 230.73) = 112.90, *p* < .001, ηp² = .70 | exact | none, same 3 choices as row 1 |
657	| 3 | *F*(2.97, 142.44) = 0.97, *p* > .4, ηp² = .02 | *F*(2.97, 142.44) = 0.97, *p* = .407, ηp² = .02 | exact | none, same 3 choices as row 1. |
658	| 4 | *F*(13.68, 1791.80) = 38.22, *p* < .001, ηp² = .23 | *F*(13.68, 1791.80) = 38.22, *p* < .001, ηp² = .23 | exact | none, it takes Type III sums of squares (Type II gives a different *F* in this unbalanced design) and the authors' discretized US data, z-scored within each populationl the other 9 effects in that paragraph also match, except that the paper prints *p* = .02 for Emotion × Modality where the data give .027. |
659	| 5 | distance = 4.24; null *M* = 8.11, *SD* = 0.97; *z* = 3.98; < 30 of 1,000,000 random pairs as close | on the stated 0–2 range: distance = 2.12; null *M* = 4.05, *SD* = 0.49; *z* = 3.99; 44 of 1,000,000 pairs. on a 0–4 range: distance = 4.23; null *M* = 8.11, *SD* = 0.97 | major | the paper says each dimension ranges from 0.0 to 2.0, and that gives exactly half of every reported distance, and the reported numbers come back only on a 0–4 range the paper doesn't mentions, and even then the observed distance is 4.23, not 4.24; the test itself (*z* = 3.99) reproduces, so the conclusion stands. |
660	| 6 | combined: 4 of 5 (not angry); movement: 4 of 5; music: 3 of 5 (happy, sad, scared) | combined: 4 of 5 (not angry); movement: 4 of 5; music: 3 of 5 (happy, sad, scared) | exact | none under the literal reading of "each of the Kreung datapoints"; measuring from the Kreung mean vector instead gives 3 of 5 for combined and for movement, two matches win by less than .005 |
661	
662	
663	Agent's own claim about success, and whether it was right: 
664	The agent said "four of the six targets reproduce exactly (including the key effect), and the other two reproduce in substance with small discrepancies, so I think the check succeeded." That's right, and its account of each discrepancy was accurate. I grade two targets differently.
665	Target 6 is **exact**, not "reproduced but fragile", because the counts match under the literal reading of the
666	paper. Target 5 is **major**, not "partly", because the method the paper states gives half the
667	reported distances. Without any hint, the agent found the 3 problems (the duplicated participant label, the unstated slider units, the doubled Monte Carlo range) and two typos in SI Table S2 (for US step size, "peaceful" has its sign flipped (+0.64 vs. −0.64), "sad" is printed as −0.49 where the data give −0.41.)
668	
669	## Time
670	
671	- Your time (hours): 2.7 
672	- Agent wall-clock time (hours): 0.23
673	- Stopped at the 4-hour cap? What remained: n/a
674	
675	## Assessment
676	
677	Is the primary result analytically reproducible? 
678	
679	Yes. The key effect (the United States Emotion × Slider interaction (ηp² = .70)) reproduces exactly
680	from the authors' data. So do the other two US ANOVA targets (the combined US + Kreung ANOVA and the
681	prototype counts). But nothing reproduced from the paper's description alone. The numbers come out
682	only after guessing the DV scale (raw units), how to handle a duplicated participant label,
683	the sphericity correction, the type of sums of squares, how to read the prototype analysis,
684	and the Monte Carlo range.
685	
686	What would have made this take 30 minutes: the analysis script, or failing that, one sentence naming
687	the software and settings (raw slider units, Greenhouse–Geisser, Type III); unique participant IDs; a
688	codebook for the column names; and the Monte Carlo range that was actually used.
689	
690	Looking at my classmate's replication, z-scored replication should be compared with .49,
691	or analyzed in raw units to compare with .70. It is because .70 is computed on raw slider units, where the rate
692	slider (30–400) dominates. In those units the Slider main effect (which the paper doesn't report) is
693	*F*(2.00, 96.04) = 863.31, ηp² = .95. That is larger than the Emotion effect the paper calls "the
694	largest main effect". Leaving rate out drops the Emotion effect from ηp² = .79 to .42. The
695	replication's analysis code z-scores each slider instead, and on the original data that scaling
696	gives *F*(9.87, 473.72) = 46.60, ηp² = .49 for the key effect, not .70.
697	
698	## AI documentation
699	
700	- Agent and interface (e.g., Claude Code, Codex CLI, Cursor): Claude Code, in the Claude desktop
701	  app (Code tab).
702	- Model and version, if the tool reports it: Claude Opus 5.5 (`claude-opus-5-5`.
703	- Context you gave it (files, instructions, any context file): one prompt and the repo. The repo held `partB.qmd` with the targets, the materials
704	inventory, `partB/data/` (Datasets S1–S2), and local copies of the article and SI PDFs. The PDFs are not in the public repo because they are under the publisher's copyright.
705	- Number of times you intervened, and the most important intervention: 0.
706	- Transcript: [partB_agent_transcript.md](https://github.com/nickmadibekov/psych251-ps3/blob/main/transcripts/partB_agent_transcript.md)
707	  (readable) and [partB_agent_transcript.jsonl](https://github.com/nickmadibekov/psych251-ps3/blob/main/transcripts/partB_agent_transcript.jsonl)
708	  (full record). They come from the Claude desktop app's session log. App-internal records were
709	  dropped, my home path and email were redacted, and the two publisher PDFs the agent read were
710	  replaced by a note.
